passage:
Pallavi: Zainab, got back from the office and tried again. Told Nani we should order groceries on the phone instead of her walking to the market every morning.
Zainab: and?
Pallavi: She went silent and folded the same towel twice. Then said "Forty years I have bought my own rice." 😔
Zainab: did you ask what worries her about it?
Pallavi: Honestly no. I kept listing how much time she'd save.
Zainab: maybe it isn't about time. My Dadi was scared she'd be cheated on weight and wouldn't know whom to scold.
Pallavi: Hmm. Last month she did ask who checks the bags if nobody is standing there.
Zainab: try one small order. Only dal, and she checks it herself when it comes.
Pallavi: And she keeps her morning walk for vegetables. Okay. Trying Saturday 🤞
Pallavi (Monday): She weighed the dal on her kitchen scale and said "Not bad." Then asked if atta can come next time 😊

qa.q: What did Nani do when Pallavi suggested ordering groceries on the phone?
qa.a: She went silent, folded the same towel twice and said she had bought her own rice for forty years.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been feeling after Zainab asked what worries Nani?
qa.a: Pallavi seems a little ashamed and newly curious, admitting to only listing the time Nani would save and never asking what scared her.

qa.q: Which step finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Ordering only dal and letting Nani check it herself worked, because it tested the change in a small way while leaving her in charge and keeping her morning walk.

qa.q: How might Nani have seen the push to order everything by phone?
qa.a: Nani may have felt it took away her control and her daily routine, and she feared being cheated with no one there to check the bags.

grounding: Shows a young working adult noticing an elder's resistance to a small household change and finding that a small trial respecting her fear works better than pushing.

passage: Every evening at the milk collection centre in Kharepatan, the old secretary Kaka wrote each farmer's litres into a fat red register, licking his thumb to turn the pages. The district had sent a tablet in March. It still sat in its box. Tushar, new on the job, had tried twice to set it up in front of Kaka, and twice Kaka had said, "Next month." The third time Tushar pressed harder, and Kaka shut the register with a thump. Later Madhuri, the accountant, said quietly, "When the bank machine failed years ago, the farmers shouted at him, not at the machine." Tushar thought about that all night. Next evening Tushar asked Kaka for one favour: keep the register, and let the evening totals also go into the tablet for one week. On Saturday Kaka ran his finger down both columns. They matched. He grunted and asked where the save button was.

qa.q: Where did Kaka write each farmer's litres every evening?
qa.a: Kaka wrote them into a fat red register at the milk collection centre.

qa.q: Why did Tushar think about Madhuri's words all night?
qa.a: Tushar felt troubled and a bit guilty, seeing that Kaka's refusal came from fear of being blamed by farmers again, not from plain stubbornness.

qa.q: What made the one-week trial work better than pressing harder?
qa.a: It kept the register Kaka trusted while letting him check the tablet against it, so the feared cost could be tested without any risk to him.

qa.q: What is it like for Kaka when a new machine arrives at the centre?
qa.a: For Kaka it feels risky: he remembers farmers shouting at him when a machine failed, so a new device threatens his standing with them.

grounding: Illustrates a young worker observing an elder's resistance to change at work and succeeding with a small side-by-side trial that respects the elder's fear.

passage: In the flat above a bakery in Tartu, Ivan, home early from the design office, was stringing lights when he brought it up again. "Babushka, the stairs at your place are getting hard for you. Let's do Christmas Eve here this year." His grandmother kept peeling potatoes. "Forty-one years it has been at my table." Ivan almost argued. Then he noticed how her knife had slowed, how she didn't look up. His flatmate Abebe had said something last week: "Maybe she's not afraid of your flat. Maybe she's afraid of not being needed." So Ivan tried another way. "What if you cook the beet soup here? My stove, your recipe, and you tell us all where to sit." She finally looked up. "Your stove is small." "Then you'll have to teach me to manage it." On the twenty-fourth she arrived early, carrying her own pot.

qa.q: What was Ivan's grandmother doing when he asked to host Christmas Eve?
qa.a: She kept peeling potatoes.

qa.q: What was Ivan feeling when he saw his grandmother's knife slow down?
qa.a: He felt a pang of tenderness and doubt, sensing the change hurt her more than he had thought, so he chose not to argue.

qa.q: Why did inviting her to cook the soup in Ivan's flat work better than insisting?
qa.a: It kept her role and her recipe and changed only the place, so she could try the new setup without losing her place in the family.

qa.q: How does the grandmother seem to see the move to Ivan's flat?
qa.a: She seems to fear losing her place as the host after forty-one years, so the move first feels like being pushed aside rather than helped.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing an elder's attachment to a family tradition and easing a small change by respecting her fear of not being needed.

passage:
Monday, 3 June. Nikita stared at the forty-page report the team sent every month. "Why do we do it like this?" she asked Sahil. "Because we always have. The director likes detail." That evening she wrote one line in her notebook: If nobody had ever made this report, what would I build? Her answer was two pages and a link to the full data.
Tuesday, 11 June. She did not scrap the old report. She sent the two-page version to the director with the long one attached and a note: "Trying a shorter format this month. Tell me what's missing." Her stomach knotted as she pressed send.
Friday, 28 June. The director's reply came: "Much easier to read. Add the regional table." The file log showed that the long attachment had not been opened once. Sahil read the reply over her shoulder and whistled softly.

qa.q: What did Nikita write in her notebook on Monday evening?
qa.a: She wrote: If nobody had ever made this report, what would I build?

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she pressed send on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was nervous, her stomach knotted, because she feared the director would see the shorter report as missing detail.

qa.q: Why was attaching the long report a smart part of her test?
qa.a: It kept a safety net, so she could check whether the feared cost of losing detail really appeared without risking the whole report.

qa.q: How did Sahil see the monthly report at first?
qa.a: Sahil treated the old way as settled simply because it had always been done, assuming the director wanted all that detail.

grounding: Shows a professional asking what she would choose if there were no default and testing one small change to see whether the feared cost appears.

passage: Yamini, you ask why I never just accept "this is how it's done." Let me tell you about the Moga branch. Your Jasleen Bua was a young clerk then, and every day at one o'clock all four counters shut for lunch. Farmers who had come on the morning bus stood in the heat for an hour. Everyone said, "It has always been this way, Jasleen." One night I asked myself: if this bank opened tomorrow with no rules, would I close every counter together? Of course not. But I was scared. The seniors would say I was disrespecting them. So I asked the manager for one thing only: for one week, two of us would eat at half past twelve and two at half past one. I was sure someone would shout at me. Nobody did. By Friday the queue had vanished, and the head cashier said he liked eating early.

qa.q: What happened at the Moga branch every day at one o'clock?
qa.a: All four counters shut for lunch while farmers from the morning bus stood in the heat.

qa.q: What was Jasleen Bua afraid of before going to the manager?
qa.a: She was scared that the seniors would think she was disrespecting them and that someone would shout at her.

qa.q: Which choice in the story let her test the change safely?
qa.a: She asked for only a one-week trial of split lunch times, so she could see whether the feared trouble appeared before changing anything for good.

qa.q: How were the farmers affected by the old lunch rule?
qa.a: They had come on the morning bus and had to wait an hour in the heat, so the unquestioned default cost them the most.

grounding: An elder recalls asking what she would choose if there were no default and testing one small change to see whether the feared cost appeared.

passage: The email arrived at 4 p.m. on Wednesday: Your seat in Advanced Spreadsheets will renew automatically unless you opt out by Friday noon. Sunaina's finger hovered over delete. She had taken that evening class for two terms, mostly because she had signed up once. Across the desk Noor said, "Just let it renew. Less hassle." Sunaina opened a blank note and typed: If I were choosing fresh today, spreadsheets or the pottery class downstairs? The answer came too fast: pottery. Then came the fear: her manager would think she had stopped taking work seriously. She had less than two days. So she asked the pottery teacher for a trial seat on Thursday night, and on Friday morning she told her manager. He shrugged. "Your spreadsheets are fine. Go get clay on your hands." She opted out at 11:52.

qa.q: By when did Sunaina have to opt out of the spreadsheets class?
qa.a: By Friday noon; she opted out at 11:52.

qa.q: What was Sunaina worried about once pottery came to mind?
qa.a: She was anxious that her manager would think she had stopped taking work seriously.

qa.q: How did Sunaina test her fear before deciding?
qa.a: She took one trial pottery session and told her manager directly, so she could see whether the feared cost appeared before cancelling.

qa.q: Why might Noor react differently to the renewal email?
qa.a: Noor sees letting it renew as the easy path with less hassle, without asking whether the class is still wanted.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking which option she would pick with no default and testing one small step before leaving an automatic renewal.

passage: Lalit, put that test paper down and sit with your Tarun Dada. You see only the two red crosses, na? Let me tell you about my own fourth class in Hisar. Our master-ji handed back the arithmetic slates. To me he said, "Tarun, eight of ten correct." I ran home like a boy who had won a kite fight. Next week, the same kind of test. This time he said, "Tarun, two wrong." I cried behind the cowshed. My mother came and asked, "How many did you get right?" I counted. Eight. Same as the week I was so happy. I felt foolish, and then I laughed. Master-ji had only turned the words around. After that, whenever someone told me what I lost, I asked myself what I kept.

qa.q: What did master-ji say to Tarun the first week?
qa.a: He said, "Tarun, eight of ten correct."

qa.q: Why did young Tarun cry behind the cowshed?
qa.a: He felt sad and ashamed because hearing "two wrong" made the test feel like a failure, even though the score was the same.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed how Tarun saw the score?
qa.a: When his mother asked how many he got right and he counted eight, he saw that only the wording had changed.

qa.q: How might Tarun's mother have seen his tears?
qa.a: She seemed to see that he was upset over words, not over his work, so she gently turned the question back to what he got right.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling happy at 'eight of ten correct' and sad at 'two wrong' as a child, though both meant the same score.

passage: The lights went out just as Devika's phone buzzed with the tuition group's results. "Battery's almost gone," she said, squinting. "Hemant, science quiz... two wrong." Hemant dropped onto the mattress and pulled the sheet over his head. "I'm useless at science." Devika scrolled with the last of the battery. "Wait, it also says eight out of ten. That's good!" The sheet came off. "Really? Eight?" He was grinning in the candlelight. Then he frowned. "But you said two wrong." "Same thing," Devika said. The phone died. Hemant lay there in the dark, counting on his fingers, eight and two, eight and two, puzzled why one had felt like a slap and the other like a sweet.

qa.q: What did Devika first read out about Hemant's science quiz?
qa.a: She read out "two wrong."

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he pulled the sheet over his head?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and ashamed, calling himself useless at science because "two wrong" sounded like failure.

qa.q: What could Devika say next time she shares a result?
qa.a: She could give both sides at once, eight right and two wrong, so the wording doesn't swing his mood.

qa.q: How might Devika see Hemant's sudden change of mood?
qa.a: She seems surprised, since to her "two wrong" and "eight out of ten" are simply the same thing.

grounding: Shows a child crushed by 'two wrong' and delighted by 'eight out of ten' for the same result, during a power cut.

passage: At the colony park in Pune, Vaibhav was throwing high catches to the younger boys before dark. Ten throws each. Chetan ran and dived and held on, again and again. "Dropped two," Vaibhav called, writing in his little notebook. Chetan's shoulders fell. He kicked the grass all the way to the bench and told his mother at the gate that he was bad at catching. Next evening Vaibhav tried it differently. After Chetan's ten, he shouted, "Eight clean catches!" Chetan punched the air and asked for ten more. On the walk home he stopped. "Vaibhav bhaiya, yesterday I also got eight." "I know." Chetan thought about it all the way up the stairs.

qa.q: How many throws did each boy get?
qa.a: Ten throws each.

qa.q: Why did Chetan kick the grass all the way to the bench?
qa.a: He felt upset and discouraged because "Dropped two" made him believe he was bad at catching.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav change the second evening, and what could Chetan learn from it?
qa.a: Vaibhav announced the eight clean catches instead of the two drops; Chetan could learn to ask for both numbers before judging himself.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see the difference between the two evenings?
qa.a: He seems to realise his wording, not Chetan's catching, changed how Chetan felt, since the score was eight both times.

grounding: Shows a child feeling bad at 'dropped two' and thrilled at 'eight clean catches' for the same result.

passage:
Class 11 maths, Thursday. Notes for the file.
The new marking software printed a line at the top of each mock paper. On Asif's it said: "Incorrect: 40%." He read it, went red, and told me after class that he was moving out of the advanced batch; maybe maths was not for him. His friend Siddharth tried to joke with him and got no answer.
I checked his paper. He had solved twelve of twenty problems, including the hardest one on the page.
Friday I asked him to stay back and showed him the same result written as "Solved: 60%, including question 18." He looked at it a long time. "It's the same paper," he said slowly. Then he asked for the batch form back.
Next step: I have asked the office to change the printed line for every student.

qa.q: What did the printed line on Asif's mock paper say?
qa.a: It said: "Incorrect: 40%."

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he read the printed line?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and discouraged, going red and deciding maths might not be for him.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: The teacher showed the same result as "Solved: 60%, including question 18", which let Asif see the paper fairly and change his mind about leaving.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt when Asif ignored his joke?
qa.a: Siddharth may have felt awkward and a little worried, since his friend was clearly more hurt than a normal bad test would explain.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager nearly quitting after reading '40% incorrect' and staying once the same result is framed as 60% solved.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Coach put the free-throw stats on the board today. Next to my name: MISS RATE 40%. Everyone saw it. My face went hot and I didn't even stay for the scrimmage. On the bus I decided I'm quitting before the district trials. Why embarrass myself?
At dinner Parveen didi asked why I was sulking. I told her. She wiped her hands and said, "So you make sixty out of a hundred?" I said yes, obviously. "That's more than half, Jagdish, you silly boy. Last month you told me the captain makes about that, and you called him good."
Same number. I was ready to quit over one word, "miss."
Going to practice tomorrow. Still annoyed, but going.

qa.q: What was written next to Jagdish's name on the board?
qa.a: MISS RATE 40%.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and defeated, so stung by the word "miss" that he decided to quit before the district trials.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do the next time a number upsets him?
qa.a: He could say it the other way round, like sixty out of a hundred made, before deciding anything.

qa.q: How does Parveen didi see the same number?
qa.a: She sees sixty out of a hundred made as more than half and a decent record, just like the captain's.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows him nearly quitting over a '40% miss rate' until the same number is put as sixty made out of a hundred.

passage:

passage:
Monday. The banner outside the metro station glowed: 80% OF OUR STUDENTS CLEAR THE ENTRANCE! Gautam stopped, took a photo, and booked a free demo class for Saturday before his train came.
Thursday. In the canteen, Arohi slid a flyer across the table. It was from a rival centre and said the same place "fails one in five students, even after a full year." Gautam's stomach dropped. "One in five? That's terrible." He cancelled the Saturday demo on the spot.
The next Monday. Walking past the banner again, he did the maths in his head and stopped dead. One in five was twenty percent. Eighty clear, twenty don't. The banner and the flyer said exactly the same thing. He rebooked the demo, and at the desk he asked a new question: "How many students joined last year, and how many cleared?"

qa.q: What did the banner outside the metro station say?
qa.a: 80% OF OUR STUDENTS CLEAR THE ENTRANCE!

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he read Arohi's flyer?
qa.a: He felt alarmed and put off, his stomach dropping at "one in five" failing, though it was the same figure as the banner.

qa.q: What question helps Gautam see past the packaging, and why?
qa.a: Asking how many joined and how many cleared gives real counts, so neither the gain wording nor the loss wording can steer him.

qa.q: How might the makers of the banner and the flyer see Gautam?
qa.a: Both seem to count on him reacting to wording: the banner wants him hopeful, the rival flyer wants him scared, using one number.

grounding: Shows a student drawn in by an '80% clear' banner and put off by 'one in five fail', then seeing they state the same figure.

passage: Vandana, you're showing me this phone screen that says "Save today only," and your eyes are shining. Let me tell you something from my college days in Goa, child. Two shops near our hostel sold the same bicycle. The shop by the church had a board: STUDENTS SAVE 400 RUPEES! I, Elizabeth, the careful one, almost ran inside. The shop by the bus stand had a board: NON-STUDENTS PAY 400 EXTRA. That one made me cross. Who likes being told they pay extra? I walked out of it in a huff. A week later my roommate, who had bought hers at the bus stand shop, put her receipt beside mine. Same bicycle, same student price, to the rupee. I had loved one board and hated the other for saying one thing. Now when a number makes me feel something, I turn it around first.

qa.q: What did the board at the shop by the church say?
qa.a: STUDENTS SAVE 400 RUPEES!

qa.q: Why did the second shop's board make Elizabeth cross?
qa.a: Being told someone pays extra felt like a penalty, so Elizabeth felt annoyed, even though a student paid the same price there.

qa.q: Which moment in the story showed Elizabeth what had happened?
qa.a: When the roommate put both receipts side by side with the same price, Elizabeth saw the reaction had been to the wording, not the deal.

qa.q: How might the roommate have seen Elizabeth walking out of the second shop?
qa.a: The roommate may have found it odd or a little funny, since that shop gave her exactly the same student price.

grounding: An elder recalls being drawn to 'students save' and put off by 'non-students pay extra', though both boards gave the same price.

passage: The phone-accessory stall at the Diwali market was shutting in ten minutes, and the loudspeaker next door was blaring songs. Pooja held up a clear case. The label said: SURVIVES 90% OF DROPS! "Buying it," she shouted over the music. Kiran turned the box over and read the small print on the back aloud: "In tests, one in ten phones still cracked." Pooja put the case down as if it were hot. "One in ten? Forget it." The stall owner was already pulling the shutter halfway down. Kiran laughed. "It's the same test, Pooja. Ninety survive, ten crack." Pooja picked the case up again, feeling a bit silly. "So the front makes me want it and the back makes me hate it." "That's the whole point of the front," Kiran said. She paid just before the shutter came down.

qa.q: What did the small print on the back of the box say?
qa.a: In tests, one in ten phones still cracked.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she picked the case up again?
qa.a: She felt a bit silly, seeing she had nearly rejected the case over wording that meant the same as the front label.

qa.q: What quick check could Pooja use at the next sale?
qa.a: She could read any claim both ways, like ninety survive and ten crack, before letting the label decide for her.

qa.q: How does Kiran see the label on the front of the box?
qa.a: Kiran sees it as packaging designed to make buyers want the case, which is "the whole point of the front."

grounding: Shows a student drawn by 'survives 90% of drops' and put off by 'one in ten still cracked' for the same test, under time pressure.

passage:
Subject: Before we send the canteen proposal
Hi Lokesh,
I read your draft for the committee. It's clear, but I think it steers them. For Anna's Kitchen you wrote "only 5% complaints," and for the current caterer "complaints in 1 of every 12 meals." The numbers aren't far apart, but the second sounds much worse.
When I made the choice for myself last night, I wrote each option three ways: meals that went fine, meals with a complaint, and the actual count out of the 600 meals we served last month. Anna's Kitchen: 570 fine, 30 complaints. Current caterer: 550 fine, 50 complaints. Written like that, the gap is real but modest, and I still lean to Anna's Kitchen.
Could we put the same three lines for both in the proposal and let the committee decide?
Lalit

qa.q: How many meals were served last month, according to Lalit's email?
qa.a: 600 meals were served last month.

qa.q: What worries Lalit about Lokesh's draft?
qa.a: Lalit is uneasy that the draft steers the committee, making one caterer sound much worse through wording rather than numbers.

qa.q: What does Lalit suggest, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Putting the same three lines, fine meals, complaints and counts out of 600, for both caterers, so the committee decides on facts rather than framing.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Lokesh might feel a little defensive at first, but also relieved to get a clear, respectful way to fix the draft.

grounding: Shows a mature colleague restating both options as gains, losses and counts before deciding, and asking that the committee see a fair frame.

passage: Thanks, Disha. So, I'm Kalyani, and two years into the job the ward office asked me to present a change: garbage pickup every other day instead of daily, with separate bins. My boss wanted me to lead with "We save forty percent of truck trips!" And honestly, that line excited me. Then I wrote it the other way: "Your lane goes without pickup three days a week." That one made me flinch. So I wrote a third version in plain numbers: ten truck trips a week become six, and each lane gets four pickups a week instead of seven. Looking at all three, I still thought it was worth trying, but I understood why people might hate it. At the residents' meeting I put all three lines on one slide. A few people shouted. But nobody could say I tricked them, and the vote was theirs.

qa.q: What change did the ward office ask Kalyani to present?
qa.a: Garbage pickup every other day instead of daily, with separate bins.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when writing the change as a loss?
qa.a: Kalyani flinched, feeling uneasy, because the loss wording showed why residents might hate the change.

qa.q: What did Kalyani put on the slide, and why was that fair?
qa.a: The gain, the loss and the plain numbers together, so residents could judge the change without being steered.

qa.q: How might the residents who shouted see the meeting?
qa.a: They were still unhappy about fewer pickups, but they could see the full picture and knew the vote was theirs.

grounding: Shows a young professional stating a change as gain, loss and absolute numbers before deciding, and presenting it fairly rather than steering residents.

passage: I was the one holding the map when Sonali called the group together at the tea stall below the pass. Two ways up: the ridge path or the valley road. She didn't say which she liked. On the back of a ticket, in neat capitals, she wrote: RIDGE: 15 of 20 groups this season made it over, 5 of 20 turned back, mostly for fog. VALLEY: 18 of 20 made it, 2 turned back, but it takes three hours longer. Then she read it out twice, once as "made it" and once as "turned back." Seema asked which one Sonali would choose. "Ask me after you've all voted," she said. I noticed she had crossed out a line first; I could still read it: Ridge = 75% success! We voted for the valley. Sonali just nodded and tightened her boot laces.

qa.q: What did Sonali write about the valley road?
qa.a: 18 of 20 made it, 2 turned back, but it takes three hours longer.

qa.q: Why might Sonali have crossed out "Ridge = 75% success!"?
qa.a: She seems to have felt uneasy that a single success figure would push the group toward the ridge, and wanted to be fair rather than persuasive.

qa.q: What makes Sonali's way of presenting the choice work?
qa.a: She gave counts for both routes, read them as both gains and losses, and held back her own view so the group could decide freely.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when Sonali refused to say which route she preferred?
qa.a: Seema may have felt a little frustrated at first, but it left Seema free to judge the numbers without leaning on the leader.

grounding: An observer describes a trek leader restating route odds as successes, failures and counts, and presenting them fairly instead of steering the group.

passage: On the first day after the summer holidays in Chennai, the new girl, Yamini, walked into Class 5B laughing, taller than everyone, her plait swinging. By lunch Lavanya had decided three things: Yamini must be the cleverest, she would never lie, and she should be Lavanya's partner for Friday's quiz. When Miss asked who would keep the class-trip slips, Lavanya's hand shot up. "Yamini should! She's so nice." On Friday the quizmaster asked for the capital of Australia. "Sydney," Yamini said, smiling brightly. Lavanya wrote it down without a second thought. It was wrong. Lavanya stared at the red mark. Nobody had ever told her Yamini was good at geography. She had just felt sure.

qa.q: Which city did Yamini give as the capital of Australia?
qa.a: Sydney.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya feel so sure about Yamini on the first day?
qa.a: Yamini's height, laughter and friendliness made Lavanya feel admiring and certain she must also be clever and honest, though nobody had told her so.

qa.q: What could Lavanya try before choosing a quiz partner next time?
qa.a: She could think about what she actually knows of a person's skills, like how they did in past quizzes, instead of how nice they seem.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel about being chosen for everything on her first day?
qa.a: Yamini might feel pleased and welcomed, but also under pressure to live up to things nobody had checked.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful new classmate must also be clever and trustworthy, so one good trait spreads into a general glow.

passage:
"Elizabeth didi, guess what, the football went missing from the PT room today."
"Oh no. Who took it?"
"Not the new boy with the big smile. He's so tall and he says good morning to everyone. He'd never."
"How do you know, Kashish?"
"Because he's nice! And he's good at everything, I'm sure."
"Is he good at maths?"
"...I don't know. Probably."
"Did you see who took it?"
"No. But the quiet boy in the corner looked guilty."
"Looked how?"
"He wasn't smiling."
"Does he ever smile?"
"...Not really."
"So not smiling is just how his face is."
"Hmm. So I don't really know anything, na?"
"You know the tall one is friendly. That's one thing, not everything."

qa.q: What went missing from the PT room?
qa.a: The football went missing from the PT room today.

qa.q: Why is Kashish so sure the tall new boy didn't take the football?
qa.a: Kashish admires him for being tall, smiling and greeting everyone, so Kashish feels certain he must be good in every way.

qa.q: What could Kashish ask before blaming anyone next time?
qa.a: Kashish could ask what anyone actually saw, as didi did, instead of judging by who looks nice or who looks guilty.

qa.q: What is it like for the quiet boy when classmates judge by smiles?
qa.a: He could be blamed and feel hurt or left out just because he rarely smiles, with no proof at all.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, friendly classmate must be honest and good at everything, while a quiet one seems guilty.

passage: Last month I voted for Zubin to be class monitor. I'm Francis, and I'll be honest: I didn't think about it much. Zubin is the tallest in our class, he laughs at everything, and he always shares his chips. So I thought he must be clever and fair too. It felt obvious. Then, on Monday, Miss left the room and Zubin had to write down the names of anyone talking. His best friends talked the whole time. Their names never went on the board. Mine did, for asking one question. I felt so cheated. Now I think being fun and being fair are two different things. Next time I'll watch what someone actually does first.

qa.q: Why did Francis's name go on the board?
qa.a: For asking one question.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when the monitor left his friends' names off?
qa.a: Francis felt cheated, having trusted Zubin to be fair just because Zubin was fun and generous with chips.

qa.q: What does Francis plan to do next time, and why would it help?
qa.a: Francis plans to watch what someone actually does before voting, which tests fairness directly instead of guessing it from height or laughter.

qa.q: How might Zubin's best friends see Zubin as monitor?
qa.a: They probably liked having him as monitor, since they could talk freely and never landed on the board.

grounding: A child looks back on assuming a tall, cheerful classmate would also be fair, until one good trait turned out not to guarantee the others.

passage: Exam week, and Keerthana had no time to think. So when the dancer she had followed for two years, the one who could spin six times on one foot, posted a video holding a jar of green powder, Keerthana believed every word. "I skip lunch and just drink this. Energy for hours!" The dancer's skin glowed, her smile was perfect, her routines flawless. Surely she knew about energy too. Keerthana ordered a jar with her birthday money and skipped lunch on Monday. By the second paper on Wednesday her head felt light and her hands shook. The school nurse gave her a banana and said she should eat proper meals and ask a doctor before trying any powder. Trisha, walking her back to class, asked quietly, "Why did you trust her about food? She's a dancer." Keerthana had no answer.

qa.q: What did the dancer say in the video about lunch?
qa.a: I skip lunch and just drink this. Energy for hours!

qa.q: Why did Keerthana believe the dancer so completely?
qa.a: Keerthana admired the dancer's flawless routines and glowing looks, so it felt safe and natural to trust her about food as well.

qa.q: What would be a wiser step when an admired person gives health tips?
qa.a: Ask whether that person actually knows about health, and check with a doctor or the school nurse before trying anything.

qa.q: Why might Trisha see the dancer differently from Keerthana?
qa.a: Trisha separates the dancer's talent from her knowledge, seeing a skilled dancer, not an expert on food.

grounding: Shows a teenager trusting a talented, good-looking dancer about food because admiration for one skill spreads to everything.

passage: Damini watched the video four times on the metro home. The cricketer she adored, fastest bowler in the league, grinning in a crisp white shirt, said, "I've put my money into this new coin. Get in early, guys, trust me." He was brilliant on the field and so kind in interviews. If he trusted it, it had to be good. That evening in their Salt Lake flat she told Rashmi didi she wanted to put all her savings from teaching tuition into the coin. Rashmi didi didn't laugh. She asked, "How fast does he bowl?" "Nearly one-fifty!" "And how much does he know about coins?" Damini opened her mouth and closed it. "He's... good at everything?" "He's good at bowling," Rashmi didi said. "Let's show this to Papa and someone who knows about money before you do anything."

qa.q: Who told Damini to get in early on the new coin?
qa.a: The cricketer she adored, fastest bowler in the league.

qa.q: Why did Damini feel the coin had to be good?
qa.a: She admired the cricketer so much for his bowling and kindness that she felt trusting and sure he must be right about money too.

qa.q: How did Rashmi didi handle Damini's plan?
qa.a: She asked calm questions that separated bowling skill from money knowledge, and suggested showing it to Papa and someone who knows about money first.

qa.q: How might Rashmi didi have felt hearing Damini's plan?
qa.a: She was likely worried about Damini's savings, but chose patient questions instead of laughing.

grounding: Shows a teenager trusting an admired sportsman about money because his talent and charm carry over to everything.

passage:
"Afreen, I'm cutting my sleep. Waking before dawn from tomorrow."
"Since when do you wake before seven?"
"Since the swimmer, the one with all the gold medals, said champions sleep less and train more."
"He said that about you?"
"About everyone! Look at him, Afreen. Medals, looks, a million followers. He obviously knows."
"He knows swimming, yes."
"Same thing."
"Is it? Chetan, would you ask a chef how to fix your cycle chain?"
"...No. Obviously."
"So why take sleep advice from a swimmer?"
"Because... he's amazing."
"Being amazing at one thing isn't being amazing at everything. Ask Ammi, or ask the doctor at the school checkup on Friday."
"Fine. But I'm keeping his poster."

qa.q: What does Chetan plan to do from tomorrow?
qa.a: Chetan plans to cut sleep and wake before dawn.

qa.q: What does Chetan's reply "Because... he's amazing" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests admiration is doing the thinking: the swimmer's medals and looks make Chetan feel sure he must be right about sleep too.

qa.q: Where does Afreen suggest Chetan get sleep advice instead?
qa.a: From Ammi or the doctor at Friday's school checkup, people who actually know about health.

qa.q: How does Afreen see the swimmer's advice?
qa.a: Afreen sees him as an expert in swimming only, so his sleep tips carry no special weight.

grounding: Shows a teenager ready to follow an admired swimmer's sleep advice because his fame and looks spread into every area.

passage: The debate society's recruitment room smelled of marker pens and samosas. Lavanya sat at the side taking notes while Manoj interviewed freshers. The fourth candidate walked in, shook hands, cracked a joke about the broken fan, and had the whole room laughing within a minute. He spoke well about why he loved debating. When he left, Manoj filled the sheet fast: speaking 9, research 9, teamwork 9, reliability 9. Lavanya looked down at her notes. Research had never come up. Neither had teamwork. She hesitated, then said, "Manoj, what did he say about research?" Manoj paused, pen in the air. "He was just... good." For the next candidate they tried her idea: one question per skill, scored before moving on. When they rechecked the fourth candidate's sheet together, research became a blank marked "not asked."

qa.q: What scores did Manoj give the fourth candidate?
qa.a: Speaking 9, research 9, teamwork 9, reliability 9.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya hesitate before speaking up?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little nervous about questioning a senior's scores, even though her notes showed research never came up.

qa.q: What change did they try, and why does it help?
qa.a: One question per skill, scored before moving on, so a candidate's charm in one area cannot spread over skills that were never tested.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when he couldn't answer Lavanya's question?
qa.a: Manoj was likely caught off guard and a bit embarrassed, seeing that he had scored a feeling of "good" rather than evidence.

grounding: Shows a peer watching an interviewer rate a charming candidate high in every skill, and scoring each skill separately to weaken the glow.

passage:
Hi Ujjwal,
You asked how the internship is going. Mostly scanning files, but today I sat in on interviews, and something stuck with me.
One candidate was brilliant in the first five minutes: warm, funny, remembered everyone's names. Afterwards our founder gave her top marks for design, deadlines and client handling. But her portfolio had two projects, both unfinished, and nobody asked about deadlines at all. It was as if her smile had filled in every box.
I didn't say anything then. Later I asked if we could split the form so each skill is scored right after its own question. The founder agreed to try it tomorrow.
I keep thinking I'd have done exactly the same thing. Would you have noticed?
Ojas

qa.q: How many projects were in the candidate's portfolio?
qa.a: Two projects, both unfinished.

qa.q: What is Ojas feeling when writing "I'd have done exactly the same thing"?
qa.a: Ojas feels uneasy and humbled, aware that the candidate's charm could have swayed Ojas as well.

qa.q: Why is splitting the form a useful fix?
qa.a: Scoring each skill right after its own question forces evidence for every box, so warmth in the first minutes can't fill in marks for skills never checked.

qa.q: What would change for the candidate if each skill were scored separately?
qa.a: Her warmth would still count for client handling, but design and deadlines would be judged on her actual portfolio, which may lower those marks.

grounding: An intern's email describes watching a founder rate a charming candidate top in every skill, and suggesting each skill be scored separately.

passage: Lokesh, listen, this is funny and a bit scary. You know I was volunteering at the mock placement day? I, Rafiq, was just the timekeeper with a stopwatch. There was this one guy, big smile, perfect handshake, he even complimented the professor's tie. The professor was beaming. Then the coding question came, and he fumbled it, honestly fumbled, but kept talking confidently. The scores went up on the sheet anyway: communication ten, coding eight, problem-solving nine. I was sitting right there. I'd heard him get it wrong. At the break I asked the professor, very politely, whether we could score coding just after the coding question, before the chatting part. There was a frown, then: "Fair point, Rafiq." In the afternoon batch they did it that way. The scores looked completely different. Some quiet people came out on top.

qa.q: What was Rafiq's job at the mock placement day?
qa.a: Rafiq was just the timekeeper with a stopwatch.

qa.q: How can you tell Rafiq felt uneasy about the scores?
qa.a: Rafiq calls it "a bit scary" and stresses having heard the candidate get it wrong, showing unease that charm had earned a coding mark.

qa.q: What did Rafiq suggest, and what was the effect?
qa.a: Rafiq asked to score coding right after the coding question; in the afternoon batch the scores changed and some quiet students came out on top.

qa.q: How might the quiet students in the morning batch have been affected?
qa.a: They may have been scored lower than they deserved, because skills were judged through the glow of more charming first impressions.

grounding: A student tells how, as an observer at mock interviews, they saw charm lift every score and suggested scoring each skill separately.

passage: I sat beside Kalyani during the quarterly reviews because I was new and meant to learn. Shankar's turn came. Everyone in the office knows Shankar: top sales every month, stories that make the pantry laugh. I expected her to tick "excellent" all the way down. She didn't. She took a fresh sheet and wrote the traits in separate rows: sales, reliability, communication, teamwork. Beside each she asked the team for one real example. Sales was easy. For reliability, someone mentioned the three client reports that came in late last quarter. Kalyani wrote that down too, without comment. When she finished, Shankar had "outstanding" for sales and "needs work" for reliability. He looked surprised, then asked what would fix it. I noticed he didn't argue. The examples were right there.

qa.q: How many client reports came in late last quarter?
qa.a: Three client reports came in late last quarter.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani write the late reports down without comment?
qa.a: She seemed calm and determined to judge by evidence, not by Shankar's charm, so she recorded the example without judging him.

qa.q: Which part of Kalyani's method made the review fair?
qa.a: She rated each trait in its own row and asked for a real example first, so Shankar's sales success couldn't lift his reliability score.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt seeing "needs work" beside reliability?
qa.a: Shankar was likely surprised and stung, since everyone praises him, but the examples let him see why and ask how to fix it.

grounding: An observer describes a reviewer separating traits and asking for examples, so a star salesperson's success does not lift every rating.

passage:
Tuesday. Salma started Saurabh's annual review on a high. His client pitch in March had been the best she'd seen, and her fingers flew: communication excellent, planning excellent, reliability excellent. She paused on reliability. What did she actually know?
Thursday. She messaged three teammates the same question: "Can you give me one example each of Saurabh's planning and reliability this year?" The replies were mixed. One said he always stepped in when someone was ill. Another mentioned two missed handovers in the summer.
The following Monday. In the review meeting she showed Saurabh a sheet with each trait and its examples beside it. Communication stayed excellent. Reliability became "good, with two handover gaps." Saurabh read it twice. "That's fair," he said. "I didn't know anyone noticed the summer."

qa.q: What question did Salma message to three teammates?
qa.a: Can you give me one example each of Saurabh's planning and reliability this year?

qa.q: Why did Salma pause on reliability on Tuesday?
qa.a: She felt a flicker of doubt, seeing that her glowing ratings came from one great pitch rather than from anything she knew about his reliability.

qa.q: What would you advise a reviewer who is dazzled by one strong moment?
qa.a: Do what Salma did: list each trait separately and gather real examples before rating, so one pitch cannot lift every score.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to read the sheet with examples?
qa.a: It seems a relief and a small surprise for Saurabh: he accepts it as fair because both praise and gaps come with evidence.

grounding: Shows a reviewer over several days separating traits and asking for examples before rating, so one brilliant pitch does not lift everything.

passage: Hafsa, you asked me how I write reviews without playing favourites. Sit. When I was new as a shift supervisor at the printing press, not much older than you are now, there was a machine operator everyone loved. Always singing, always first to help unload the paper. I was about to write "outstanding" in every column. Then the old foreman, grumbling as usual, said, "Akash, what has he actually done on the machine this year?" I had no answer. So I made myself a rule that day. Each column gets its own evidence: one real example for speed, one for accuracy, one for safety, and I asked the other operators too. His safety column turned up a near-miss at the paper cutter that nobody had logged. He got "excellent" for team spirit and "needs training" for safety. He was upset for a day. Then he thanked me, because the training kept his fingers safe.

qa.q: Where did Akash work as a new shift supervisor?
qa.a: At the printing press.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when the foreman asked what the operator had done on the machine?
qa.a: Akash felt caught out and uneasy, seeing that the "outstanding" came from liking the operator, not from evidence.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed how the review turned out?
qa.a: Akash's rule of one real example per column, plus asking the other operators, which uncovered the unlogged near-miss.

qa.q: How did the operator react to his mixed review?
qa.a: He was upset for a day, then grateful, because the safety training kept his fingers safe.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to rate each trait with its own evidence so a well-liked operator's charm did not hide a safety gap.
